Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 28 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the introduction by Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland of discriminatory legislation designed to deprive Canadian citizens in that province of their right to freedom of association and to membership in the trade union of their choice, and the imperative need for the government to formulate immediately a policy to guarantee basic human rights and fundamental freedoms to Canadian citizens in every part of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minisier of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have forgotten the first part of the question. I believe the hon. member asked for a report on the situation. I do not think there is anything I can add for the information of the house which is not contained in the press today. But I am glad the hon. member has raised this other question, because I think in fairness to the house the situation should be clarified.
There have been statements in the press and elsewhere during the last few days that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has changed its position from that which it adopted when the so-called memorandum was initialled some time early in February. At that time I did not feel I was free to discuss the memorandum because the understanding was that it was to be kept confidential until the matter was completed. However, since

Inquiries of the Ministry the wording of this memorandum has appeared in the press on several occasions I do not think anyone could accuse me of a violation of confidence if I were to put a paragraph from it on the record.
With the consent of the house I should like to put on the record a short statement from paragraph 3, subparagraph 1 I think it is, of the agreement which was initialled early in February. I am reading from the English translation. The original agreement was initialled in French, but I am assured the translation is absolutely accurate. This is how the paragraph reads:
The association of producers, due to the role which its members play in the areas of public opinion and public service, and because of the particular position which these members occupy in the C.B.C., undertakes to maintain its independence from any third person, labour union or group of unions, but the association has the right, of course, to ensure for itself advice of a technical nature and assistance from such third person or groups.
That was one paragraph of the agreement which was initialled some time early in February, after these discussions, in fact. Latterly it appeared that the producers felt the agreement would permit them to affiliate with the C.C.C.L., despite the fact that there is this specific statement in the agreement that they were to maintain their independence. As a matter of fact the producers issued a statement which reads:
There is no question of the association of producers breaking all relations with the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. The normal machinery of our association's affiliation to this labour organization is not completed, even though a request to this effect had been voted before the strike by a general meeting of our membership.
It is evident, however, that we now intend to respect both the spirit and letter of the agreement which we have arrived at with the C.B.C. and that our relationship with the C.C.C.L. will be regulated by a special statute-
There may be some misunderstanding as to the meaning of this word "statute", that is whether they mean a statute or a regulation.
-different from that of regular unions affiliated to this organization and taking into consideration the independence which we have agreed to maintain.
The problem arises, of course, as to how, in one document at one time they state they should be absolutely independent of any union or group of unions, and in the next breath they say they are going to be affiliated with the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, although the machinery of that affiliation has not been completed. It is in an effort to clarify that question that the delay has taken place. Right from the beginning the question at issue in this strike was independence of any union, as the house well knows, and the corporation thought the problem was resolved when this agreement was initialled.
Now it develops that there is a real question of whether this independence is a play on words-I am not suggesting it is a play on words-as to the difference between a trade union and a management union, and the producers apparently feel they are entitled to have a management union but they deny any thought whatever of a trade union. The corporation has asked them to clarify that matter and that clarification has not been forthcoming. This is where the matter stands at the moment.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Can the minister say whether a decision has yet been made as to the site of any new federal penal institution for the maritime provinces?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SITE OF NEW FEDERAL INSTITUTION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; a decision has been made. Our problem in connection with an institution in the maritimes is twofold; first, to meet the overcrowding now existing at Dorchester penitentiary, which is the only federal penitentiary in the Atlantic area; and second, to plan for the situation which will exist when arrangements are made to take over additional prison responsibilities from the provinces.
To help prepare these plans the correctional planning committee has completed a survey of the Atlantic area. They have reported to me that it is their opinion that a site should be selected as soon as possible which is capable of development to meet

both the requirements I have mentioned and that the Springhill area which they visited possesses to a remarkable degree those basic features that are necessary as a site for a correctional institution; and they have recommended it as the logical location.
The Springhill area has accordingly been chosen as the site. There is still a good deal of planning to do in preparing a national system of penal institutions; therefore I cannot say when the full scale development of this site will be undertaken. Since, however, we have to deal with the overcrowding situation as a matter of urgency, a start on development will be made at the earliest possible moment.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, I am very glad, as I know all hon. members will be, that in this case the logical development of our plans enables us also to make some contribution to the restoration of an area which recently suffered an appalling and tragic disaster.

The position is this, Mr. Chairman. But not only are these people inadmissible; the effect is that their families' afe also denied admission, because entry is not granted to any family a member of which is suffering from tuberculosis, mental illness or some other incapacity.
Obviously the situation of these people can become desperate if they are required to spend periods of years in camps for unsettled persons or alternative United Nations accommodation in Europe, with no solution in sight for the problem. There is no hope of their getting out of the camp and being accepted in any country other than the one in which they are residing as non-settled cases, and as long as the illness persists they are required to continue living in these European camps or other United Nations accommodation.
There is one alternative, but it is obviously unattractive to many. The members of some of these families who are not incapacitated by illness may come to Canada under certain conditions providing they are willing to leave the ill member behind, and many families are not willing to make this sacrifice. In the high commissioner's report it is stated that a recent survey has shown that among the nonsettled refugee population there were 4,700 difficult cases in camps including all family members, and at mid-summer of 1957 there were 16,300 non-settled difficult cases in alternative accommodation.
Certain countries within the United Nations have recognized the existence of a problem, have waived the regulations which make those people inadmissible, and have instituted special programs to take care of a number of them. Probably the best example of this is the program undertaken by Sweden and Denmark in conjunction with each other, in which they took 200 difficult cases and provided for them under a special program. The Swedish representative reported to the third committee of the United Nations that 200 of those cases have been successfully treated, brought to a cure and integrated into the community in both Sweden and Denmark.
I feel that this is a continuing problem that can never be resolved unless nations

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration such as Canada and others are prepared to institute special programs to deal with a particular situation. I would suggest that perhaps Canada is in a better position than most nations to undertake a program on behalf of tubercular cases in particular. If my information is correct, the incidence of tuberculosis in Canada has been considerably reduced in recent years, so much so that in one province at least a sanatorium that had been in operation for a great many years has been closed, since it is not longer necessary, and other similar institutions are operating at less than capacity in other parts of the country. Improved medical care and treatment, better preventive programs and so forth, have brought Canada into this relatively favourable position.
I feel, therefore, that Canada should join with Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, France, Italy and some of the other countries that have recognized the difficult situation of those refugees and institute on a trial basis-and I would suggest in the first instance on a trial basis only-a program designed to provide for the difficult cases and in particular those who are suffering from tuberculosis. This could mean, Mr. Chairman, that as few as 50 tubercular cases accepted into the country would provide a solution to the problem of 200 and more people, because there may be in many instances one tubercular case in a family unit. If we could provide a program of treatment, care and cure for one we would to some extent automatically solve the problem of a larger number.
I realize, of course, that it is not a simple program. There are complexities involved, and it would require greater expense for the handling of individual cases than would ordinarily happen. This is why I would suggest, particularly in view of the employment situation in the country at the present time, that the matter be studied now and if it could be instituted this year, if conditions are favourable, that it be done. But if it cannot, and if it does not seem feasible this year, preparations could be made so that such a program could be instituted at a time that is appropriate.
I believe there are a number of successful programs in addition to the Swedish one that Canada might use as a model for any trial program; but I also believe that the best case study we have in this particular regard is the project undertaken two years ago by Sweden and Denmark. Consequently it would not be necessary for the government of Canada to enter upon such a program without having the opportunity to understand exactly what was involved, what

costs were likely to be encountered and the degree of success that would likely be attained.
I think it can be readily understood by all hon. members of the committee that life in a refugee camp, or in any impermanent accommodation, without any other solution of the problems of the people involved, can become extraordinarily sterile because those people have no prospects of a solution of their individual problems. Naturally as it is borne in upon them that this life could go on for them without any future prospects of any attractiveness whatever, they are bound to become despondent. Those who are ill are bound to find those conditions weighing heavily on their minds, which would prejudice their chances of recovery and, in any event, the United Nations probably does not have available to it the sums necessary to effect complete cures of those cases which are well advanced or stubborn in response to treatment.
I think several countries such as Canada, which have a good record in the treatment of tuberculosis in particular, could help to solve this continuing problem. At least, Mr. Chairman, I feel that Canada is in a sound position to study the problem; for as long as the prospects of acceptance and resettlement are denied those people, as long as they have little hope of restoration to health, if they lose confidence in the good faith and good intentions of the people to whom they have turned for refuge, they can become prey to the influence of disaffection and hostility.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the influence of even a few who believe themselves to any degree to have been betrayed can spread fear beyond the bounds of a few European settlements. I fear that growing disaffection will be the consequence of failure to take the steps which are necessary to solve the problem of the difficult cases of those refugees. Therefore I would ask that Canada study the successful programs undertaken by certain European countries, which in many cases are not as favourably situated to handle those problems as we are, to see whether there is not some way in which we might undertake a similar program for the relief of at least a limited number of those difficult cases in Europe. Then on the basis of that trial program we can see whether Canada can institute a continuing program and consequently influence other countries to do the same, until the problem that exists in the European camps is eliminated forever.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke on the very lofty and humane

appeal he has just made to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. This is not a new problem; it is a problem with which I know the Department of Citizenship and Immigration of Canada, as well as those of of other countries, have been wrestling for some years now in an endeavour to clear up the old hard core of refugees who are still wandering about with no place to go. It is something which has come to the attention, I am sure, of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and we can only hope that the government will rise to the great heights of being humanitarian about this problem and will bring about as speedy a solution as possible.
Perhaps this too might fall into the category of the government at last recognizing the importance of large-scale immigration into Canada. During the nine or ten years I have had the privilege of being a member of the house there have been debates as to the advisability and necessity of encouraging large-scale immigration into our country, and I am pleased to see that at long last recognition has been given to that principle. It has been given by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and by the present Minister of Finance. The principle has also been recognized by the Prime Minister.
Only a short while ago I had occasion to refer to some remarks the minister made in what I believe to be her most recent speech outside the house, in which she emphasized as eloquently and as forcibly as anybody possibly could the importance of encouraging immigration into Canada. Let me read what she said on January 14, 1959 as reported in the Montreal Star:
Immigration minister Ellen Fairclough said today that immigrants have helped to bolster the Canadian economy by their consumer buying, by establishing new businesses and industry and by bringing money into the country. Mrs. Fairclough denied that immigrants were taking jobs away from native born workers.
I am sure hon. members will recognize that by that statement the minister has completely exploded the myth that immigrants who come to Canada take jobs away from Canadians. She was very clear and categorical; but in the event that there is any doubt on that score in the mind of any member let me continue, for purposes of emphasis, with what she said on that occasion:
Occasionally we hear that immigrants take work from native born Canadians and aggravate unemployment; this notwithstanding the oft-expressed view of reputable economists that there is little or no connection between immigration and unemployment.

It is very encouraging for us to know that. In making her statement she gave details as to the amount of manufactured goods that new immigrants have consumed over a certain period and the amount of purchases they have made, so there should be absolutely no doubt in anybody's mind but that large-scale immigration would certainly stimulate employment in Canada.
I have also referred to the categorical support of the Prime Minister. In a report emanating from Toronto on April 26, 1957 I find that the Prime Minister said that Canada must have new population through immigration if it wants to hold and develop its resources. He went on to say at a press conference at the Canadian ethnic press club that "we must either populate or perish".
I therefore say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to hon. members in the house, particularly members of the government: Pay close heed to these words, "we must either populate or perish", words uttered by no less a personality than the Prime Minister himself. As I said previously, this view was also supported by the Minister of Finance when he brought down his last budget, and I feel that at long last the principle of large scale immigration into Canada is being accepted by the entire country.
In the event that some might think the labour unions still persist in their fear that immigrants might take away jobs, I am happy to say that this view has been exploded by economists who, as the minister has stated, certainly have made a study of the matter and are familiar with the problem. I should add in all fairness that the Prime Minister went on to make the statement that the only limit on immigration should be the capacity of Canada to absorb newcomers into her economic life. He added that Australia's forward looking immigration policy has produced the conclusion that it can absorb 4 per cent per year of its total population and that such a yardstick applied to Canada would establish a figure of 640,000 immigrants a year or more than four times the number that came to Canada in 1956.
There you have the Prime Minister of the country stating in clear and categorical terms that if Canada followed the yardstick employed by Australia it could absorb 640,000 new immigrants a year. In the light of what the minister herself and the Prime Minister have said about large-scale immigration, it is important for us to have a look at the figures for a moment to see what the government has accomplished in this regard since it took office. I now quote certain figures. In 1957, 282,164 immigrants came to Canada; and accepting the new trend toward large

Supply-Citizenship and. Immigration scale immigration one would have expected that In 1958 there would have been: a tremendous upsurge if that policy had been followed through. Instead we find a lamentable situation. In 1958 only 124,825 immigrants came to Canada, or less than half the number who came in 1957.
That is something that has puzzled me. The government has accepted the principle that large-scale immigration is- necessary and urgent. They have accepted and recognized the principle that immigrants do not take away jobs from Canadians. Where was there any hectic activity to increase immigration in 1958? Something happened in a mysterious way. I address myself to the minister for an explanation. What happened to her theory, her desire, her belief in large-scale immigration which resulted in this lamentable drop in the immigration figures?
It has been pointed out that there was a lower number of immigrants from the United Kingdom thdn ever before. This is something that has to be explained. I am wondering whether the immigration program is controlled administratively through the strictness of immigration regulations. I realize and can say from personal knowledge that without any doubt we certainly have most competent and efficient immigration officials. I have met them in Canada. I have met them in the various countries of Europe. I think they are of the highest type and are most conscientious, competent and capable men.
I feel, however, that their hands are tied. They are rigidly bound by regulations. In the light of this new approach to large-scale immigration I now want to make a plea to the minister to review the Immigration Act so as to allow the officials who meet prospective immigrants more latitude in dealing with them and more authority in making decisions about these matters, rather than having them bound rigidly by a discipline which is almost military in its form. They cannot go beyond the regulations.
Let me illustrate. An applicant for immigration comes before an official in Paris, London or Rome. The official sees the man, talks to him, is impressed by his appearance and his education, as well as his financial means. Here is a man who is most competent. He is well trained, a specialist in some field. Unfortunately that immigration official has no authority to say, "In my judgment this man would be a good immigrant for Canada, and I will issue a visa". He has not that latitude.
Why has he not that latitude? It is because this applicant may come from a country against which restrictions are imposed because of relationship. This man may not be the brother, father or son of . somebody in

Canada, and under our Very strict regulations this might make it impossible for that mSn to come to Canada. You may have, on the one hand, the son of a Canadian citizen who applies to come to Canada and who is incompetent, who is impoverished, Who has no skills and no training. However, under our regulations he is admissible to Canada. The other man who is so extremely competent and most desirable is not eligible to enter Canada. I therefore again urge the minister to see that her officials abroad, who meet these immigrants and talk * to ' them, who look into their eyes, who hear their replies and who cross-examine these men, have more latitude.

I want to point out something else to illustrate why I believe a review of the immigration act is now due. The last time it was revised was some years ago, and in the light of the change in the entire theory of immigration I think the act should be revised now, especially if we really do want to populate Canada. There should be a revision if we want to take the advice and leadership of the Prime Minister, who said "populate or perish". I consider that a root trend in government policy in connection with immigration, and in the light of that root trend our immigration regulations should be so redrafted that they could meet this trend. It will be impossible to do so under present regulations, even with the best will on the part of all our immigration officials and the best will on the part of the government.
Let me give some illustrations. I draw to your attention that under the Immigration Act parliament has given authority to the government to make regulations, and it is interesting to note the grounds upon which anybody may be denied entrance to Canada. These grounds are not contained in our law, they are not contained in the act which came before parliament and which parliament examined. All these prohibitions and all these permissions are contained in the regulations which parliament never saw. The regulations were prepared by the government or by departmental officials and were enacted by order in council. I think this is rather unfortunate. I do not know whether or not these regulations could be held illegal by a competent court.
However, these are the regulations which govern and control immigration into Canada, and which never came before the House of

Commons or any committee of the house. I want to deal with them. For example, people are admitted from some countries if they are unmarried children under 21 years of age. If a child were 22 years of age that child would not be admitted. I ask hon. members, is an unmarried child 22 years of age less beloved by its parents than an unmarried child 20 years of age? The 20 year old child is admitted, but the 22 year old child is not admitted.
Then, too, the unmarried orphaned nephew or niece under 21 years of age is admitted. It is quite possible that an orphaned nephew or niece who is over 21 years of age is not admissible into Canada. Well, we want to be sympathetic and we want to consider these things. Here are anomalies in our laws which are difficult to accept. You have too, Mr. Speaker, the fact that a father who is over 65 years of age is admissible, or a mother who is over 60 years of age.
Now, I ask this question on whatever ground you want to approach it. If a father is 64 years of age or if a mother is 59 years of age and they want to join their children in Canada, why should there be that prohibition? Why should we say, because you are not yet over 65 you cannot come to your children, or because the mother is not over 60 she cannot join the family here? These are anomalies in the law which I do not criticize. I feel that at the time they were enacted they were created in order to control the flow of immigration from various countries. However, if we believe in the humanitarian grounds to which reference has been made, certainly a revision of regulations of this kind would be well justified.
Let me give you another illustration, and on this I make a direct appeal to the minister. Brothers and sisters of Canadian citizens who came from Poland are admissible into Canada. If you are not a Canadian citizen, even though you have lived here for 10 or 15 years, you cannot bring your brother or sister from Poland to Canada. Well, perhaps that is a privilege that is extended to the brothers and sisters of Canadian citizens, but I should like to appeal to the minister. If a person comes to Canada from Poland and has been here for three years or four years and then finds he would like to bring a sister from Poland to Canada, then I would appeal to the minister to extend that category. I would say that people who are landed immigrants in Canada, whether or not they are yet naturalized, should be permitted to bring their brothers or sisters into Canada.
At one time, and not so many years ago, even brothers and sisters of Canadian citizens were not admitted into Canada. I remember that I was on a delegation which waited on
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the minister and deputy minister and appealed to them to allow brothers and sisters to emigrate to Canada. We had a good reception, and both the minister and the deputy minister at the time agreed to amend or arrange the regulations so as to allow brothers and sisters to enter Canada provided the applicants in Canada were Canadian citizens.
I now appeal to them again. There are not many more of those people left in Poland. They have practically all come. There may still be some left in Poland whose brothers and sisters in Canada are not yet Canadian citizens. It would be in line and consistent with the minister's desire and intention to be considerate and humane about the matter to extend that category.
The same thing applies to another group. The department showed much compassion and consideration to the unfortunate refugees who were compelled to get out of Egypt. Some of those who also had to get out of Poland and made their escape out of that country-they were able to get out; it is not always easy to get out of those countries- made their escape into France or into Austria. Under existing regulations these refugees who flooded those countries are not permitted to come to Canada unless they sit around somewhere in Europe for at least two years.
At the time I could understand the purpose of that regulation, but all those reasons are now fairly well exhausted. I think the minister and the department, having regard to our desire to populate Canada, should extend that category to include refugees and escapees from Poland and from Egypt. I know it would be a humanitarian act, and it certainly would be much appreciated. It would also be consistent with the appeal made by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke.
I should like to raise another point, Mr. Chairman, and deal with the question of those who have come to Canada as visitors. I appeal to the committee to take note of this painful situation, which I think requires to be remedied. I now speak of cases with which I am personally familiar. A man comes to Canada as a visitor. He is in Canada for a month or two and then asks for permanent landing. He is examined. He is found to be a man of means, of education and of competence, but he is told, "When you left Europe you were asked whether you were going to Canada as a tourist or whether you were going to Canada with the intention of settling there, and you said you were going as a tourist". The charge is, "You did not tell us the truth", and the man is told, "Go back to Europe and make your application there". Strictly speaking that

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Draconian application of the law and the regulations could be right; but having regard to common sense, fairness and the economy of the thing itself, I do not think that a man, after he has been in Canada, decides that he would like to remain here and makes his request, should be told to go back to Europe. It is not merely a question of the expenditure of $1,000. One gentleman with a large capital to bring to Canada-in fact he had it here- told me, "If Canada does not want me I can find other countries to which to emigrate''. He said, "I will go to Australia, or I will go to South America". The Prime Minister at one stage said that we have lost many good immigrants through strict interpretation of the regulations. I should like to give that quotation:
The Conservatives, he continued, will end the arbitrary and unjust interpretation of immigration regulations which have been a feature of Liberal immigration policy.
At another place he made another statement. I just cannot find the quotation at the moment, but he stated that Canada has lost a great many good immigrants by a harsh interpretation of the regulations. I feel that if we in Canada are approaching an era in which we propose to expand our immigration, the minister and her officials should take a second look or another look-and a good one-at our regulations which I find are sharp, harsh and Draconian.
I know that many of our immigration officials are most sympathetic and have expressed that sympathy; but unfortunately they say, 'My hands are tied; I must follow the regulations". The regulations are harsh, Mr. Chairman, they could stand much revision. If only we had that confidence in our immigration officials abroad to allow them to exercise their discretion based on their training, their knowledge, the fact that they have met the prospective immigrants; and if they find they are desirable immigrants, to give them authority to issue a visa-that is the way in which we will get good immigrants, rather than have them sit around in some city in Europe, write to Ottawa and ask for a permit.
Of course there are certain requirements that are basic. Every immigrant must be in good health and must have a good moral record. These are basic requirements. Certainly every immigrant must, after investigation, be acceptable to Canada. He must not be a communist. Once these basic requirements are met, what difference does it make whether, as a father, he is 66 years of age or 64 years of age, or whether as a brother he is 21 years of age or 20 years of age, or whether he comes from this country or that country? If he is a desirable
[Mr. Crestohl.l
immigrant, if he has the means, if he is useful, if he can help to build the economy of Canada, I believe we should give the immigration officials abroad the authority and power to exercise their discretion and their sympathy. I do not think that the department will make any mistake if it will show full confidence in all its immigration officials abroad and not have them held tightly by a series of Draconian-I repeat the term -or harsh regulations.
Maybe that sort of thing was necessary at the time Canada's policy was restricted or selective immigration, but certainly my appeal is supported by the Prime Minister, by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and by the Minister of Finance. If we are now taking a new trend in immigration, let us make it possible by giving our officials the necessary authority.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak quite briefly this afternoon. What I have to say represents the opinions of some people in my constituency who are members or supporters of all parties in this house, who are much concerned about the question of immigration.
First of all I want to thank the minister for her willingness to give information when it is sought and to reply at considerable length to letters from a member who on occasion is extremely troublesome. I want to compliment the senior staff and the officials of the immigration branch. I think anyone who has had anything to do with this problem realizes that they have some extremely difficult and trying situations with which to deal. You always do when dealing with human beings.
I also want to include the local officials in southeastern British Columbia, whom I know very well indeed and who have been very harassed on occasions in the last year or two by the burden imposed upon them through unexpected immigration policies and things of that sort. I have admired the way they have carried on their duties, at considerable inconvenience and discomfort on occasion, and I might say I am of the opinion that Ottawa does not always quite realize what it is asking the local officials to do. In some cases they have been asked to do a bit too much.
Having made those complimentary remarks, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about immigration, because I have discussed this matter with some of the people in the labour movement, at veterans' meetings, women's associations, and with business people and a good number of people on the street. I associate with my people; I like to find out what they are thinking. I suppose

it is because of the recession-I think that is the correct term-of the last year that there is more concern about this problem than there has been for some years.
We in this group, as the minister knows, stand for an immigration policy planned according to the capacity of the country to absorb immigrants. I think that is a very sound stand, and it is a policy which, in one direction or another, can be made elastic to meet changing circumstances. I think when considering immigration at this time we have to realize we have nearly half a million unemployed Canadians in Canada. While we cannot expect to occupy this vast land without providing opportunities for people from other lands, our first responsibility is to the people of Canada, particularly under these circumstances. In our opinion only those immigrants should be brought to Canada, with the exception of a few refugees I want to mention later, who can go to assured employment or who are not going to be a charge on the public exchequer because they are going to be cared for by relatives or sponsors until they obtain employment, and are assured of housing without displacing Canadian citizens.
The hon. member who just preceded me argued that under present circumstances immigrants do not take jobs away from Canadians. Mr. Chairman, I want to say that is absolutely untrue and not according to the facts. I can speak with some knowledge on this matter because I have had cases brought to my attention. I would like to mention one case of a veteran who fought for this country, not against it, for five years, now living in the city of Nelson, who was unemployed for several months. He was an electrician who registered at the national employment service and was unable to obtain employment. An immigrant-and I do not blame him-coming from central Europe obtained a job as an electrician within three days of arriving in Canada. He took the job which the Canadian veteran should have had.
Another illustration. I happen to be associated in a very small way in the lumber industry and meet quite a lot of people interested in that industry and engaged in it. I know of a case where five immigrants obtained employment in one lumber company's mill, while in a neighbouring small village there were a good number of Canadians seeking employment who had registered with the employment service. I have had numerous illustrations brought to my attention of that type, particularly during last year. So it just is not correct to say that immigrants do not take jobs away from Canadians; under certain circumstances they
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration do. I have been asked to bring this to the attention of the ministry by some very good citizens in my constituency representing all parties, and I might tell the minister that very prominent supporters of her party have written some rather caustic letters in the press about these matters.
Why do they get these jobs? As I say, I am not blaming the immigrants at all. They get jobs often before Canadians who have been unemployed for some months. I see the former minister of immigration looking at me. I am sure he will differ with me more and more on this point as I proceed with my remarks. But why do they get these positions? Because the average Canadian registers at the national employment service and waits for a call for a job. He has not the money to travel all round the country. The immigrant gets a special service. The officials of the department travel all over the country looking for jobs for immigrants. I do not blame them; it is their duty, and it causes them quite a headache. In one case they went to a small company with which I am acquainted and begged the manager to take on one or two of these people. They said, "They have dumped down a number of people and we have to distribute them somehow." Then if someone is needed in the mills or in the woods at that moment the manager often says he will give them an opportunity.
I might say that this company gave three or four the opportunity, but as they were only able to make $12 a day splitting fence posts they resigned after four days and went to live at the government of Canada's expense at a hotel in Nelson. That is a fact, because I followed the case up. We have had a number of illustrations like that, but of course they are a few of the bad eggs.
So the Canadian unemployed are placed at a disadvantage under these circumstances. That is why, on behalf of a great number of people in my constituency, I do urge that this question be given very careful consideration so that we do not have the situation where immigrants are brought to this country and forced to compete with Canadians, take their jobs away on occasion, or live at the public expense until they can find employment.
I think the formula I have outlined is sound. They should be brought to this country when there is assured employment or when they are going to be cared for by relatives or sponsors until they have obtained employment, and when they have an opportunity to obtain satisfactory housing without competing for scarce housing with Canadian citizens. Having said what I intended to say on that question, I now want to say a few words about the representations made by Chinese Canadian organizations with respect to the admission of certain relatives. I want to express my support for the briefs of those organizations. I have had a lot to do with a small number of Chinese Canadians over a long period of years, and I must say I never found that these people came to the government for assistance or support. I do want to express my support for the plea made by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke for the admission of a certain number of refugees. I think in that connection, and on strictly humanitarian grounds, we should give some consideration to their plight and accept our share in liquidating this long term and unfortunate problem. Now I come to my concluding remarks. Last year I was going to ask the minister a series of questions with respect to the immigration of Hungarians into Canada, but as I happened to be called out of the house I did not have that opportunity. However, I wrote the minister a letter in which I asked the questions which I had been requested to ask by persons in labour organizations, by veterans and by students at the University of British Columbia. The minister replied at some length and completely answered my question and I thank her for that. In her letter she mentioned that as of September 8, 1958, the total approximate cost had been $14,413,929.05-I like that 5 cents. I will not go into a complete breakdown of the costs.
The hon. lady proceeded to answer the other questions I had been requested to put to her. She wrote me as follows:
In reply to your third question, the Sopron forestry faculty was brought to British Columbia from Vienna at a transportation cost to the Canadian government of approximately $105,000 and provided with accommodation and maintenance at a cost to the Canadian government of approximately $347,190


-an approximate total cost of $452,190, or about $1,482 for each member of the group of 305. The cost is approximate only because these refugees were accommodated in immigration hostels at different times since their arrival and while there, the cost has been assessed at $2.25 per person per day.
With regard to your fourth question, of the 305 members of the Sopron forestry faculty, there were 190 students, 28 members of the faculty and staff, and 90 dependents (3 dependents were also students).
I have always been amazed at the large size of this faculty in view of the fact that Hungary is a grain-growing country and has a relatively small forestry industry. While all parties in this house supported the estimates required for the bringing of these people to this country under emergency conditions, and I think we have been very generous indeed, I am one who under the present circumstances thinks there comes a time to call a halt. The enthusiasm with respect to this migration has considerably lessened in recent years no doubt due to the lapse of time and various contacts and incidents that arose in various places across Canada in connection with some of these people.
I was interested in listening to the appeal of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on behalf of the Sopron faculty and students at the University of British Columbia for assistance for them to complete their education at the university. I well understand his good intentions in that respect. However we have already been very generous. We brought all these people here and paid their expenses but when we are asked to do what he proposes I suggest we should remember that there are hundreds of young Canadians who have not been able to finish their university course in the last year owing to the fact that they were unable to obtain employment, last summer particularly, between the closing and the opening of the universities.
We have young Canadians who were former students of the University of British Columbia and who were unable to continue their courses at the university this year because they found it impossible to obtain employment during the summer months. I believe we should give consideration to that fact and therefore I have been asked to express the objection of a good number of people who are supporters of all parties in this house, as I said before, to this proposal while we have young Canadians unable to continue their university courses because of being unable to obtain employment. I think we should treat all these people at least on an equal basis. I cannot support giving this ultra-generous treatment to this small group of people when we know, as I have already

mentioned, there are a good number of young Canadians unable to continue university courses in Canada this year.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned the fact that if we did not complete this operation it would serve to give the soviet government the laugh on us, as it were. I think that was the purport of the hon. member's words. The government of Russia, he suggested, could be critical of our being unable to complete this project. I do not think the government of the U.S.S.R. gives tuppence whether we complete it or not, and I believe we have to view the question in the light of the money we have available and also in the light of our responsibilities to young Canadian citizens first.
On behalf of the people who have mentioned this to me I wish to take exception to the payment of the fees for these people to complete their courses at the University of British Columbia unless we are willing at the same time to do the same for the young Canadians who live in British Columbia and who are unable to complete their courses for the very same reasons.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I may be permitted to say a word or two in reply to the last observations that were made in a spirit which is not the usual spirit of the hon. member for Kootenay West. I need not say I disagree completely with every word he said about the Sopron faculty. I find it very difficult to reconcile the utterly ungenerous attitude he took in this matter with his appeal to the minister for generosity to other refugees which immediately preceded it. I am going to say to the hon. gentleman what was said last summer by the hon. member for Assiniboia who sits beside him when this parliament voted $40 million for the grain farmers of western Canada. The hon. member for Assiniboia rose and said, "I hope nobody is going to say that this should not be done unless something is also done for the fishermen."
It seems to me the suggestion that we should not do something that is good in itself because something is not going to be done for somebody else is a very dubious argument. This parliament practically since the time of the Korean war has voted approximately $2 billion a year to the defence and security of the free world. Why? Because we believe there is a struggle going on in the world between those people and nations who believe in freedom and those that want to subjugate the whole world to a communist tyranny.
It so happened about two years ago that owing to certain events that took place in Hungary 200,000 and more people left that country and went to Austria. It is true that 66968-9-104
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration among them were a limited number who fled in the early stages because they had belonged to the communist secret police. There were a few bad eggs among those who came to Canada and when I spoke the other day I said that no one was more pleased than I was to see these bad eggs go back. But it seems to me that the hon. member for Kootenay West has completely ignored what the real situation was at the time the action we are now discussing was taken. These 200,000 Hungarians simply could not stay in Austria. The Austrian state with only 6 million people simply did not have the resources to look after them. Canada, in concert with most of the other countries of the free world, did its share to see that these people were accommodated elsewhere because most of us in this country at that time, I think, believed that if the free world was so bankrupt of statesmanship and wealth that it was going to allow these people to go back to Hungary and be deported to Siberia it would be just as serious as losing any other engagement in the cold war and perhaps more serious and demoralizing to all the people behind the iron curtain who long for freedom.
It happened that among the people who came to Austria from only 10 miles across the Austrian border and from an area that is forested and has been for years, from one of the oldest forestry schools in the western world, was the whole forestry faculty of Sopron university. I heard about this faculty when I was in Vienna. I went personally to see them. First, I got in touch with my colleague of those days, the minister of fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, who got in touch with the leading members of the forest industry in British Columbia and received assurances of a good deal of help for those people, particularly from the Powell River Company who did a magnificent job of receiving the forestry faculty and getting them started on life in Canada. Now, there was-I do not say an undertaking because there was not an undertaking-I have had this out with the faculty myself-a feeling that this faculty would remain intact and the students would be allowed to complete their studies. My view then, and my view today is that when we had the opportunity to get those young people already half trained professionally rather than just taking the run of the mine of the same number of Hungarian refugees, we were doing a good job for Canada and I still think so, and I believe that in the long run that is going to be demonstrated.
No doubt, like other students, there will be a few among them, a very few I think, who will not turn out to amount to very much but I believe that most of them are going to

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be a great success and a great credit to Canada. I think myself that the people of British Columbia are very lucky to have got people already half trained on whom otherwise it might have had to spend thousands and thousands out of taxes for education.
The hon. gentleman talks about Canadian students who are not able to get back to the University of British Columbia because they were not able to get jobs last summer. We all regret cases of that sort. We know there have been some cases of that sort, but let us remember what the situation is for these students who, except for their own little community, have no family connections in Canada. They have no connections; they had no previous contacts here in Canada. At a time when we do have a recession, at a time when we do have unemployment, at a time when the hon. gentleman himself, in the earlier part of his speech, was complaining that immigrants were coming here and taking the jobs of Canadians, a proposition about which I could say something but I will refrain, it does seem to me that it would be a very short-sighted thing, even from the point of view that the hon. gentleman himself has in mind, if those students were suddenly deprived of the means of continuing their studies and were thrown on the labour market in the middle of the winter. It does not occur to me that anybody in British Columbia would benefit from that at this time.
No problem would ever have arisen, as I am sure the hon. gentleman would agree with me, if the conditions in the forest industry of British Columbia had remained in 1957 and 1958 what they were in 1955 and 1956. When the assurances were given to Mr. Sinclair, as they were, they were given on the assumption, which many people made, that the kind of buoyant condition of employment in the forest industries was going to continue. Unfortunately it did not continue and that caused the problem.
Most of the funds required for the support of those students are being provided by other means but the University of British Columbia has made what for a great rich country like Canada is a very modest request for a small amount of help out of the national treasury. I think myself that we would look pretty small not only in our own eyes but in the eyes of other countries, if we feel that because a few people here and there are going to criticize us we cannot behave like adults in the world and deal generously with this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to join with those who have preceded me in complimenting the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration on her forward look on immigration. The hon. member for Cartier
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
referred to the speech which the minister made recently in the city of Montreal. The speech indicated that of the immigrants who were admitted to Canada during the past few years, relatively few are in the ranks of the unemployed.
I rather liked what the minister had to say regarding the often heard remark that immigrants are taking jobs away from the native born, which is an old prejudice. Besides being unreasonable it is absolutely unjustified. Therefore, I cannot agree completely with the hon. member for Kootenay West who made reference to immigrants displacing Canadian-born from their jobs. I heartily endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke with regard to the refugees in concentration camps in Europe at the present time. This fact proves conclusively the importance of adopting a realistic immigration policy based on the ability of the country to absorb immigrants.
Mr. Rhys M. Sale, president of the Ford Motor Company, made a speech recently in the city of Toronto from which I wish to quote a few paragraphs because I think it is very apt. He said:
[DOT]'Canada should be able to absorb a halt million people annually, from natural increase and from immigration, without the slightest pressure. True, we may have periods of economic adjustment when unemployment may become a temporary problem, but we should not allow that to have too much influence upon our immigration policies. We have abundant room for people, abundant resources to be developed. We have too much of everything to justify undue restriction of population growth."
Since 1945 Canada has received 1,800,000 immigrants and already more than a million of their children have been born on Canadian soil. "Ninety per cent not only emigrated from their homelands of their own free will, but came to Canada by choice," Mr. Sales said. "They could as easily have gone to other countries, such as Australia, which would have welcomed them with open arms. Instead they caught the image of Canada and decided this was the land of freedom and opportunity in which they preferred to make a future for themselves and their children. It should make us proud to have them with us."
Then, on February 24, 1959, Mr. W. A. McFaul, superintendent of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, made a speech in Montreal from which I wish to quote a few paragraphs which are very revealing. Mr. McFaul said:
Of 124,800 immigrants to Canada last year only 18,600 were helped by the department in finding work on the open labour market.
The remaining 106,200 were dependants, sponsored workers and immigrants admitted for selfestablishment, he said in addressing the Royal-mount Kiwanis club.
It was too little known that only a relatively small proportion of the total number of immigrants seek employment on the open labour market. Each year Canada was acquiring valuable skilled workers

and professional men whose education and training had cost Canada nothing and whose presence tended to offset the loss of trained Canadians through emigration. Mr. McFaul said in the past nine years immigrants had established in Canada a total of 2,358 small business enterprises by purchase at a cost of $27,602,500, and 84 by rental. Immigrants in 1958 alone bought farms in every province except Newfoundland.
Of course, all this sounds very good but what are we doing about it? Does the government have a realistic immigration policy? Notwithstanding all these encouraging statements, I have reason to believe that as far as European immigrants are concerned the doors are shut tight, with few exceptions, owing to the present unusual unemployment situation throughout the country aggravated by lay-offs as a result of the suspension of the activities of Avro. I do not advocate a wide open immigration policy but I do believe that persons sponsored by responsible citizens who are able bodied, of good character and in good health should not be barred from entering the country. I know of specific cases where applications of prospective young immigrants who were sponsored and guaranteed employment were not approved. I should like to ask the minister what the present policy of the government is with respect to such people.
I would also urge a more sympathetic approach by the government to Asiatic or coloured applicants for admission to Canada. People of Asiatic descent have made a substantial contribution to this country and I feel that if others of these races are allowed to enter they too will contribute to the growth and prosperity of Canada. If we are to develop the northwestern part of our country, about which we hear so much, then let us adopt a policy of settlement based not only on present but on futui-e needs because if this country is going to take its place in the world-the pioneers of half a century ago predicted that the twentieth century would belong to Canada-then we should have such a policy.
I have the highest respect and admiration for the present minister because she is efficient and has undoubtedly conducted her department in such a manner as to gain for her not only the respect of the house but of Canadians everywhere, and if she will present a policy to parliament I am sure it will be approved unanimously. I want to wish her and her officials in the department every success because we are very much interested in their work. I am very much interested because in my own constituency we need immigrants of the right sort to settle on land which is entirely suitable for colonization and farming. The land is there waiting for somebody to come there and work it.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak only briefly in what has been a very interesting and thoughtful debate. My purpose in rising is to echo as forcefully as I can the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. I think there are perhaps two fundamental reasons why his suggestion, which has been endorsed by a great many members of the committee this afternoon, should be considered very seriously by the minister and her department and by the government. First, I am informed by some of the doctors in the house that facilities in the form of hospital space are available for the treatment of tubercular patients. I know that over the years Canada has prided itself on winning the war against tuberculosis. No doubt there are other diseases in the same category. The mere fact that we have been able to accomplish this victory against what was once a dread disease should give us all the more reason to assist- these people from abroad who are in the unfortunate position of being victims of it.
The second reason why I support the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke is simply that since the war I believe a good number of thinking Canadians have developed what might be called a bad conscience about the immigration policy of this country. In certain countries abroad we have become known as healthy body snatchers. We have taken the best of the unfortunate victims of the war and the aftermath of war in Europe and we have left the infirm and the ill there to fend for themselves. I say that this has given rise to pricks of bad conscience in this country.
Certainly we should do whatever is possible to put Canada in the same position as some of the countries of northwestern Europe which have not only taken the well unto themselves and made them citizens but have also permitted the sick to come along with their families. I think this could be accomplished by the minister and the department by establishing some sort of policy. Admittedly it would have to take into account the medical facilities available in different parts of Canada and have regard to those provinces in which there are facilities for the treatment of tubercular cases. It would also have to

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion immigration to this country should be allowed on the basis of the country's capacity to absorb newcomers. I am expressing my own personal views.
Under present circumstances, however, I feel it would be better to curtail immigration. This, as I see it, is the only sound approach to the matter.
At no time in the past was the former government willing to consider the country's interests, nor those of the immigrants, and Canada's gates were thrown wide open at a time when many Canadians had trouble finding jobs. As a result, Mr. Chairman, unemployment grew worse and, bitter discontent was felt among immigrants who. instead of improving their lot, had sometimes made it worse.
Need I mention, Mr. Chairman, that in the federal riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, and more particularly in St. Paul l'Ermite, some immigrants staged a hunger strike?
We should not bring in people who will be unable to find a job or will be taking jobs away from Canadians with families. Very often, immigration is a source of economic and social wealth for a country. However, it would be illogical to think of welcoming to Canada people seeking work when a great many Canadians are in a similar predicament.
Socialists, for instance, who are forever talking of "liberty", sometimes reply that we have no right to bar the way to people who want to settle in Canada. To my mind, this is wrong. Admission to Canada is to the foreigner a privilege and not a right. And this privilege should be granted only in cases where it is considered unlikely to affect the general interest of the Canadian nation. If a foreigner is free to leave his own country, a Canadian should also, and perhaps more particularly, be free to enjoy a decent standard of living here at home.
Mr. Chairman, most immigrants who have come over in recent years have become excellent citizens. Yet a number of them
[Mr. McCleave.l

find it hard to make a living. Others have gone away dispirited and now indulge in anti-Canadian propaganda as false as it is detrimental. All that would not have happened if the former government had been alive to its responsibilities and had asked people to this country-

Mr. Chairman, I very humbly leave these suggestions, which I am making in a personal capacity, to the consideration of the house.

come to this country as long as the country can absorb them, and I favour the principle that this government keep their number within the bounds of our absorption capacity.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make my contribution to this debate. I do not intend to speak at any length. First of all, I should like to express my support for the remarks made in the house today by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. I think the hon. member put forward an idea which is worthy of investigation and which has many positive features to it. He referred to those "lost souls" in the camps who are still left in Europe, primarily in Germany. A great many of these people would be worthwhile citizens of Canada if they could be rehabilitated because many of their relatives and friends are to be found in this country.
I was very happy to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax because he referred to some of the things which I had contemplated mentioning. There is no question but that in the field of tuberculosis Canada has made great progress. We do have a great many experts in this field. We are happy to note that our conquest of this disease has reached a point which is a matter of pride for all Canadians. I believe we might well utilize these institutions, if at all possible, for the rehabilitation of some of these unfortunate people. We do make great contributions in many ways through other agencies toward humanitarian work. I might mention the Colombo plan as an example. This would be a further contribution which Canada might make in a field which is so close to the hearts of so many of the Canadian people.
There is one other point I should like to mention and that relates to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I am very happy on this occasion to agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in the statements he made concerning the students who are today attending the University of British Columbia, and who came here as a faculty from Hungary during those fateful days when Hungary was attempting to obtain her freedom from communism. I think I should point out to those hon. members who may not agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that these people came to us in the prime of life. I presume that today most of them would be in their late twenties. We have never had to spend money on them for public school or high school education. There were no baby bonuses paid for them and some of their university educational costs were paid before they came here. Before very long these
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration students will be making a real contribution in their professional capacity to the Canadian economy.
There may be criticism of the fact that we are giving them this extra help. However, when you consider the need for professional men in this country I think that can be justified. During the past few weeks we have heard about this problem in connection with the cancellation of the CF-105 and the possibility of losing some of our professional men in this field to other countries. Here is an opportunity for Canada to gain professional men in another specific field related to an industry which is of great importance to this country.
On the whole, I should like to say that I agree with most of the remarks which have been made by some hon. members today relative to the immigration problems which face us. I might mention that undoubtedly the great boom which has occurred in Ontario, the province from which I come, has been due in no small measure to the fact that we have had a larger number of immigrants come into this area. These immigrants have accounted, I believe, for a greater production of materials and undoubtedly this has been one of the major reasons that Ontario has enjoyed a tremendous expansion.
In conclusion I only wish to reiterate that I agree with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, the hon. member for Halifax and, in the case of the students at the University of British Columbia, with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I believe that these several items can be considered primarily on humanitarian grounds. I am sure that as Canadians we are all anxious that Canada's record not only amongst Canadians but among those beyond the shores of this country should be clear in this regard. In the particular case of the Hungarian people I would say that the western world, feeling as it did and coming to the aid of the Hungarians during those trying days, can do no less than try to rehabilitate and assist in some tangible way some of those unfortunate people who were able to get away from communism. In this regard I am hoping that something further can be done to show our appreciation of those people and of what they represent, and in this way to show to other people, who may be looking at Canada and her attitude in international affairs, that we are a humanitarian people.

Mr. Chairman, I object to an hon. member stating as was done this afternoon by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, that we should curtail immigration. In my opinion, ours is a vast and rich country, of immeasurable natural wealth, and I believe we have an obligation to share this wealth with other citizens of the world. Christian charity commands us to share this wealth lavished upon us by a bountiful Providence and personally I am convinced that by letting in citizens from other parts of the world, we are not making ourselves poorer but that on the contrary, we are adding to our riches.
Attempts have been made in certain quarters to suggest that people coming here from other parts of the world are taking jobs away from native-born Canadians. Mr. Chairman, I cannot concur in this view, because whenever a new citizen is admitted into this country, thus adding to our population he needs food and shelter and this, in my opinion, creates employment. This new fellow-citizen not only does not make us poorer, but adds to Canada's wealth. The more people there are in this fine and great country, the less it will cost to provide the people of Canada with the services they require.
In closing those few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I wish to pay tribute to those who have come from other countries to live among the people of Canada. We are greatly indebted to them and I am pleased to mention among them a man who immigrated to Canada and gave us our present Prime Minister. I am happy to note that the Prime Minister comes from an immigrant family to mention but that one case.
In business, in industry and other related fields, we find people who have come from other countries of the world to give us their support. We are proud to have them among us, and I hope that in the future, the government will continue to apply, with a sense of Christian charity, the policy whereby we open Canada's doors to citizens from other parts of the world for our country's enrichment.

to the countless numbers of Chinese families who also are refugees from communism.
