I was not the minister, and it was not my responsibility to settle the strike. However, there is a strike going on right now in Montreal and it is under the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). And it is not a matter of two or three persons being unemployed, but of thousands of people who are starving because of the present government's failure to act. There is more urgency in settling the present strike than in harking back to small local strikes in the constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the house is enjoying the calm and complacency of the debate going on in regard to immigration at the present time. It gives a little diversion and is amusing. But probably we should go back to the broad aspect of this immigration policy to which everyone seems


to want to subscribe. I would like to say that the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke started off on the right keynote by appealing for an improvement in existing conditions. In the same way, so did the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for High Park and the hon. member for Cartier. They all contributed to the debate in the light in which they believe the position to be. The hon. member for Kootenay West presented the case as he saw it, and I think he was perfectly justified in mentioning certain conditions. But I suggested that the policy of the department which has been carried out by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will meet with the approval of the house generally, and the policy she is pursuing is in thorough keeping with what has been asked of her.
I think it was suggested, if I remember rightly, that a movement was afoot by labour organizations in this country to restrict immigration. Repeatedly they have asked that there be a stop to, or a restriction placed on immigration in such times as are confronting us generally, and without getting into the controversy about who is right or wrong, I must say that that policy has been continued from the previous government. They found, notwithstanding the fact that our labour force in the country is more than it ever had been before, that when they encouraged immigration in such large numbers during the year the hon. member for St. Denis had reference to we were able to absorb them into our labour force. Nevertheless, we have inflation and unemployment, and we are trying to solve those problems. Everyone is convinced that this country cannot go on the way it is with our present population. The problem we are confronted with is that our cost of living is very high. We have one of the highest standards of living in the world, and therefore to a certain extent we have priced ourselves out of world markets. The only thing we can do is to make sure we have markets of our own by having a large population in Canada, whom we are able to look after and provide with employment.
On that broad basis I think the immigration policy of the department should be: We will take in as many as we possibly can. It is said that there was criticism offered of this department when we were in opposition. That is true; but if you examine the record you will find our plea was for more immigration, but on a broader basis. Some of us thought that there was not an equalized admission to this country of the different ethnic groups of the world. Personally, some of the observations which have been made could stand a little more discussion.

I am perfectly satisfied that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the former minister of citizenship and immigration, did the best job he could while he held that portfolio. Of course, the hon. member has many shortcomings and qualities we do not like but we must give him his just due and I know that the milk of human kindness flows in his veins. My experience with him has generally been satisfactory. He was always willing to listen to the views of hon. members of the opposition and he gave them sympathetic consideration when he could. I have found him to be fair and we have gotten along together fairly well. I am sure that wherever possible his suggestions will similarly receive sympathetic consideration on the part of the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
The hon. member spoke of the problems concerning the admittance of people from Hong Kong. We all know the difficulties involved in that question. I am convinced that the department will work out a solution that is to the best advantage of Canada without restricting unduly the right of these people to come to Canada. What the hon. gentleman said about the Chinese people who seek admittance is quite true. They are a most likeable people and are extremely law-abiding. They try to fit in well in this country. It may well be that they like to indulge in a harmless little game of fan-tan among themselves but I do not suppose that we in Canada can claim to set a perfect example because we too occasionally like to indulge in a game of chance and we should not be too critical of them. Nevertheless the matter of the admittance to Canada of people from this country is one requiring great discretion on the part of the department and I am sure the policies of the department at this time represent a logical continuation or sequence to what was done in this respect during the period when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate held his portfolio.
I cannot resist commenting on the exchange of ideas that took place between the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with respect to the Sopron faculty and the fact that students in British Columbia and many other parts of Canada are unable to continue their university courses because of their being unable to obtain employment. On the face of it it appears as if there should be an adjustment there but it is always interesting to hear all sides of a story and I took pleasure in listening to the remarks of those two hon. gentlemen and the hon. member for High Park. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred to the fact that last year the government introduced measures valued 66968-9-105
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration at $40 million to assist the farmers of western Canada and said that the hon. member for Assiniboia in talking to him privately at that time, expressed the hope that no one would suggest that the same should be done for the fishermen. This brought a thought to my mind and I checked back in the record to verify it. I remember that last year when the house had under consideration assistance to the maritime provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in terms of thermonuclear development the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said the government should do something similar for Newfoundland. It occurs to me that there is a strong similarity between these two situations and that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate drew an unfair comparison when he contrasted the attitude of the hon. member for Kootenay West today with the attitude held at that time by the hon. member for Assiniboia. When one places an argument before this committee one often fails to present the full picture and one may unwittingly tend to draw unfair comparisons.

Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. member does not want to be unfair and I do not want to be controversial but may I state that in both those cases I did not oppose what the government was doing. I supported what the government was doing in both cases. The difference between me and the hon. member for Kootenay West is that he was opposing something I thought was good.
You held them up.
I did not hold them up. Nothing has been done about them yet.

I will accept the explanation of the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, but I must comment that in the heat of debate one sometimes tends to make comparisons for one's own benefit. The attitude the member for Bonavista-Twillingate took is somewhat like that of small boys who say, "If you do not do for me what you are prepared to do for somebody else, I will pick up my marbles and go home." While the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and others from the province of Newfoundland did not oppose what the government proposed with respect to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia they were most vocal in stating that the government should also have included Newfoundland.
I will support that, too.

I believe the same remarks could apply to the situation to which I made reference concerning the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West. What was said by the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration hon. member for Kootenay West illustrates a problem with respect to immigration today. It has frequently been said that the triangular shaped area in Canada embracing Windsor to Quebec and north to North Bay contains approximately two-thirds of the population of this country. As immigrants continue to enter Canada either under a policy of sponsored or unsponsored immigration it will be the duty of the department to encourage those people to disperse across the nation rather than crowding into our more heavily populated area. There must be long range plans and consideration must be given to the distribution or dispersal of immigrants across the nation so that our relatively uninhabited areas may develop and industrial expansion take place in areas where it is needed and our natural resources may be constructively exploited to meet the needs of a growing economy and an increasing population. If this is done under a mature policy Canada will not have to rely too much on exports and eventually will become more self-sustaining. The north will be opened up, the population and industrialization of the western provinces will increase and consumption of our surplus commodities at home will be assured. We should avoid having our presently developed areas attempt to assimilate additional population through immigration.
I have raised this question because we have been welcoming many immigrants to this country. On the advice of labour leaders the government has restricted quotas of immigrants for the time being but we want as much immigration as we can intelligently handle and it may well be that an expanded program of immigration will take place in the future. We require immigration so our natural resources will be developed faster and many of the problems that now beset us because of under-population, including the problems of the railways, will be more rapidly resolved. On the other hand we are eager to preserve our freedom and our high standard of living and we must take no action through an open door policy of immigration that would jeopardize our liberties through allowing into the country people whose ideological concepts and ways of life are in direct conflict with the traditions and freedoms we cherish, enjoy and seek to preserve.
In the future when the shadow that hangs over our heads has passed away I am sure the government will adopt policies of immigration under which will accrue the greatest benefits to Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I
should like at this time to speak for a few moments on sponsored immigration. I firmly believe that in order to maintain our economy


and keep abreast of the pace of expansion it is necessary to have a steady flow of good immigrants to Canada. However, I am well aware that if we open the gates wide at the present time many people may come to Canada and find themselves facing difficulties in terms of securing employment and becoming established.
I have mentioned immigrants coming to this country being sponsored by their friends and relations here in Canada. When I speak on their behalf I speak for a large group of Canadians, especially new Canadians, who are trying desperately at the present time to bring to Canada from different parts of Europe their friends and relations who are living under troubled conditions. I know that at the present time practically all the immigrants who are coming here are coming under sponsorship. I should like to make some suggestions to the minister and I make them in a friendly way. Sometimes I have disagreed with decisions which the minister has made, and she might feel that I am a little hard. However, that part of Canada known as the Niagara peninsula, which I represent, is a fine place in which to live and there are a great many people from different parts of Europe who wish to come to live there. There are some countries in Europe from which it is easier to get to Canada than from others. They are allowed to bring mothers, fathers, wives, husbands, brothers and sisters. From some countries they are allowed to bring nieces and nephews and from others they are allowed to bring fiancees and also brides and husbands, but for some other countries the restrictions are very tough. I think the regulation should be the same for all countries. May I give an instance?
I have a letter here which I received from the department in connection with a family that is trying to get here from Poland. We were making very good progress. They had been approved as far as the local offices here were concerned and we were expecting to get word any day that they were on their way. However, I am informed today that the family here has been advised that the group they were sponsoring from Poland, which consisted of a father, mother and two daughters, were in this position. It had been discovered that one of the daughters is 20 years of age and therefore she is barred from coming to Canada. I think this is very unfortunate; it is a situation which should be corrected because how can a family come from Poland and leave a daughter 20 years of age who is really a juvenile in law?
I should like to make this point at this time. Our regulations require some changes

so that a family of that kind would all be allowed to come here rather than debar one because she is 20 years of age? I could recite a good many cases that have come to my attention, cases that I have worked on but they are all more or less the same. In so far as some countries are concerned, as soon as a child or any person gets over a certain age he cannot come here. I could refer to another case which is similar. A girl is 21, and of course she is completely debarred from coming here to a good home and an opportunity for a real education and a chance to make good in this country.
There is also the question of fiancees. I think this is a matter to which we should give some consideration. I might say that I was involved in a case not so long ago where I found it was permissible for sisters to come to this country but not fiancees. This particular person arrived here as a sister but she was actually affianced. I thought that when she was here that would be the end of it, that we could write it off; but unfortunately we ran into a problem with the monsignor of the catholic church who said, "It is fine, the girl gets in here but you know we cannot marry brothers and sisters so you will have to do something about it." I should just like to say to the minister that everything turned out all right. The girl got married and they disappeared, and I burned my file with as much glee as a Presbyterian minister when he burns the mortgage on the church when the debt is paid.
I am not going to make a long speech on this, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to make a special appeal for sponsored immigrants. I suggest that the regulations be broadened in such a way that not only close relations but those who are probably just on the fringe could come here. After all, when most people come here they come under sponsorship and the party who is bringing them out undertakes to see that they become established in this country and to look after them until such time as they are able to become settled and make way for themselves. I do not see why we should not open up that type of immigration and bring more people of that kind to this country.
I might also make some remarks about Chinese people who are British subjects from Hong Kong. I know this is a matter which is controversial but nevertheless it has been my pleasure to know people of this kind who have landed in this country for one reason or another and then find that they have to be deported. It is very unfortunate that they should be deported, especially at the present time when the 66968-9-1054
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration regulations permit them to make their application in Canada rather than go back home again and try from there.
There is also the question of the Chinese people who came to Canada in years gone by, made good and have quite a stake in the country. They wish to bring their children to this country. There again they are up against the problem that if the children are over 21 years of age they cannot come here. Hong Kong is at least a part of the British commonwealth of nations. We should give some consideration to special cases of that kind. I do not say that we should open up the gates and allow a great many Chinese people to come here; I am against that but in certain cases we should perhaps do better than we are doing at the present time.
This is about all I have to say at the present time, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I discovered last year that if one wanted to get a full answer to questions from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration one had to pose his questions early and the minister would pick them up. I would like her to report later on what the situation is at the present time in the two countries of Italy and Poland in so far as people coming out here are concerned. I know that the difficulty in Poland is largely one of making arrangements with the present Polish government to expedite the movement of people who are eligible to come here to join relatives but who have blocks thrown in their way by the government of Poland. I should like to have a report on how that is coming along and whether there is any noticeable improvement.
I gather that the problem in Italy, and it has been brought up several times, is the fact of only having one centre, that at Rome, and because so many people are eligible to come here the facilities in Rome are not able to process them with any speed. I should like to know from the minister what the backlog is now, whether it has been reduced recently and whether there is any intention to increase the staff in Italy in order to move more of these people out here who have been proven eligible to come.
There is one other point in connection with immigration from Italy which I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and I have done so before in another form. I refer to the kind of assessment that is made of prospective emigrants to Canada in so far as their political background is concerned. I have talked recently to two Canadian businessmen of Italian origin who have been over there. They say that in some parts of Italy, especially in the south, there is a tendency

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration for anyone who has opened his mouth at all at any time in the last 15 or 20 years to be labelled as a communist. These men both told me that they felt the department should take a very close look at any adverse reports that may come out of southern Italy with respect to the political complexion of people because so often people who really have no link or tie with the communist party are labelled in that manner.
Furthermore, many people who have taken part in political activity within the ranks of the social democrats are labelled as communists by the parish priest and other officials who make reports to the Canadian immigration department. I agree with the hon. member for Danforth who made the point that we need close screening in order to keep out people with radical or left wing persuasions of the communist kind, but from at least two cases I have encountered in my constituency I certainly have the feeling that people are being prevented from coming here because of political activities or sympathies that have been assumed to be communist when in fact they are really not that at all.
There is one other matter I have taken up with the minister and about which we have had certain discussions. I refer to the minister and her officials being placed almost in the role of Dorothy Dixes or intermediaries in lovelorn affairs.
I thought you were the specialist in that.

I think everyone tends to think that they are. The minister knows the cases of which I speak. It does seem to me that it is time the department tried to work out some crisper form of regulation with respect to people coming to Canada to get married because the minister will be aware of a couple of cases where true love seems to have faded as soon as the arrival of the affianced in the particular community took place. I understand there has been a tendency for this kind of thing to become a racket in some ways. There is really no love or romance at all in some of these arrangements. I know that in Europe it is often argued that this kind of arrangement makes for a much more solid base for marriage, but on the other hand we have these people coming out here to Canada supposedly intending to go through a marriage ceremony and very often the marriages do not take place. I think it would be very interesting if the minister could give us some statistical information on what happens in these cases. I do not want to give publicly the details of two cases that I am aware of because we are still in hopes that something may be done about them.
Are you Cupid?

But it is very awkward when someone in Canada spends money and goes to a great deal of effort to bring out a potential husband or wife and then discovers when they get here that true love really was not the impetus at all. It was simply a chance to partake generally of the Canadian scene. I hope the department will look into this matter.
There is one final point I wish to make with regard to immigration. It has to do with the particular ethnic group that happens to be the largest in our region, people who have come from Finland. One point that has been brought to my attention by people in the Finnish community with respect to immigration from Finland is that its character has changed to quite an extent. Anyone who drives round the lakehead region will realize that a great deal of the backbone of the whole community, so far as farming and bush work are concerned, is provided by people of Finnish stock. That is as it should be when one recognizes that Finland is an area about the same size as my constituency with roughly the same climate, the same amount of arable soil but with a population of approximately seven million whereas the constituency has a population of 90,000.
The Finns are experts at logging and a combination of bush farming and logging in their own country which makes them ideal immigrants for our part of the country and for the whole boreal forest band. But what has been noticeable about recent Finnish immigration is that so many of the people are from the cities. Because these people are such a premium to our area I wonder if a really strong effort could not be made when immigration does broaden to go after the people in the Finnish country districts in order to get more of them out here. We know that the majority of them will tend to come to our part of the country because the Finnish community has a solidarity based upon its own cultural institutions and its own newspaper that makes Port Arthur a magnet much more than any other community in North America for people from Finland.
The whole lakehead area is aware of how much this kind of immigration has meant to the region. We believe that we have land for agricultural development which would really benefit from this type of immigrant. From conversations I have had with a number of people in the Finnish Lutheran Church I know that they would welcome the opportunity to co-operate by making contacts in the rural districts of Finland in

order to get more of the kind of people over here who can step right into our woods areas and who will have the background and the experience that no other type of immigrant from Europe really has, with the possible exception of some from Norway.
In the boreal forest area we have a very peculiar kind of farming and logging problem that is only paralleled in Finland and Russia. We do not expect to get any immigrants from Russia and we have had these people of a very high standard from Finland who have meant so much to our country. I would ask the minister to take under active consideration the matter of going into the rural districts of Finland so that we can get more of that type of person over here. As a corollary to these remarks may I say I do not want to give the impression that I think the people from the cities of Finland are not worth-v/hile immigrants, but in terms of usefulness and being a real boon to the area they have no advantages over people from any other part of the world while the people from the rural areas of Finland certainly have.
In conclusion, I should like to say that I hope the minister will be some time in this particular portfolio. I, for one, have found her very agreeable in so far as immigration and citizenship problems are concerned. I hope she manages, in the next few years, to make a real mark of the best kind in this particular role she has before she is called away to what I imagine will be the higher responsibilities that her general abilities, I am sure, will warrant.

I should like to make one or two additional observations, if I may. I am sure the discussions this afternoon on these estimates, in the presence of the minister and her senior officials, are very helpful in enabling them to observe how the whole house, with very few exceptions, has seized upon what I should like to call the new obiter dictum from the Prime Minister with respect to immigration. The house has seized upon his words to the effect that Canada must have new population from immigration if it wants to hold and develop its resources. Practically the whole house has seized also on the Prime Minister's warning to Canada that we must either populate or perish.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I hope too that the house and the departmental officials, as well as the minister, may accept two other warnings that the Prime Minister gave. I am now quoting from the Montreal Gazette of April 27, 1957, which states:
The Conservatives, he continued, will end the arbitrary and unjust interpretation of immigration regulations-
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
He also said with equal strength in a statement appearing in the Globe and Mail on April 27, 1957, and I quote from that article:
He-
That is the Prime Minister.
-pledged a more vigorous immigration policy would step up the flow of skilled immigrants, end the "bureaucratic" interpretation of the immigration act, and ensure that humanitarianism would be considered more often in handling immigration applications.
I quote these two admonitions or what I might call promises from the Prime Minister because they go hand in hand with this plea for increased immigration. That is why I emphasize them at the present time, so the minister and her officials will also be aware -I am sure they are already aware-of the Prime Minister's desire that these immigration regulations be not interpreted so restrictively, so harshly and right to the letter of the law, but that a more generous interpretation of these regulations be made. In that way, I am sure that the house will give effect to the Prime Minister's desire that we have an immigration policy that is expansive rather than restrictive, as he advocated in his speech on April 27, 1957.

I just want to make a couple of brief observations before the hon. lady speaks, as I hope she is going to do. I should like to echo what was said by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke at the beginning of the debate. I have in my hand a copy of an article by Mr. Stanley Burke, who is a correspondent I think for all Southam papers but this appeared in the Citizen of February 13. I am not going to inflict it on the hon. lady or on the committee because I daresay the hon. lady has at least read it. The article is along the lines of what was said by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke.
I think we should make an effort as Canadians to take some part in this refugee year, and try to do a reasonable and proportionate share to draw to a conclusion this refugee problem once and for all in the hope we are not going to face the kind of world in which new refugee problems will be created, though that might well be. There is one real difficulty about this which the minister knows as well as I do, and that is once one year has passed, according to present practice and present policy-at least, it certainly was the policy when we were in office-any responsibility for relief or assistance or anything of that sort ceases to be a federal responsibility and becomes a provincial responsibility. In view of that situation we took the view, when we were in office, and so far as I know the hon. lady still does, that we should not bring

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people into a province who were suffering from some kind of disability, temporary or permanent, unless the provincial authorities agreed and unless reasonable provision was made for treatment.
I do not believe, having regard to our federal constitution, that it is very reasonable for a government to take any other attitude than that. It is not right for us to deliberately create problems for the provincial governments. I know that I did have some difficulties, particularly in the case of the hon. lady's own province, and I hope that may be changed. I noticed, perhaps it is the shadow of events to come, that in that province they have now set up a citizenship branch in their own government. I must say I am from Missouri about this and I will have to be shown that there is a more humane attitude than there was when I was in office. Perhaps the hon. lady has more influence with Queen's Park than I had. There is where at least half of these cases arise, and I think if we are to do anything effective about relatives, particularly elderly relatives-there are a great many of them-of residents of Canada who want to come here, not to go into the labour market but merely to live in their old age with their families and who, because they had a spot on their lung or something of that sort, are denied admission, it might be useful if the hon. lady could get an agreement with the provinces. I do not think we necessarily have to have agreements with all of them because in some provinces there are practically no cases. Perhaps some sort of policy could be worked out in this refugee year. I do not think we should take all of them, but we could do a reasonable share in this field.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee will agree with me that the discussion we have had this afternoon has been most interesting. If anyone needed proof of the diverse problems which confront this department, I am sure that has been furnished in the remarks of the members today. I shall attempt to answer a few of the questions that have been put to me. I hope that if there are any specific questions to which hon. members would like answers, and which I inadvertently overlook, they will tell me.
There are two or three things I should like to say, and one of them is in reply to the hon. member for Cartier and his last plea for a humanitarian approach to this problem. It has been my aim ever since taking the responsibility for this department to administer the affairs of the department in a humanitarian way. Of course, there are cases where the decision is not only difficult but possibly unfortunate. I can well understand that hon. members who present cases that

they feel are very strong cases must be disappointed if the decision which is made is an adverse one. However, that is one of the responsibilities of this office and one which I cannot shirk.
A number of pleas have been made for co-operation in this international refugee year. This is, of course, a problem which will have to be solved by this department in conjunction with other departments of government, notably the Department of External Affairs. This is a problem which we are looking into at the present time. However, I should like to point out to members of the committee that while this hard-core problem is there and has been there for some time, it presents a peculiar problem, as has been mentioned by several hon. members, and just a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
This matter of bringing people into this country to go immediately into hospitals must be cleared, I think, with the provincial authorities. I am sure that all members interested know that in various sections of the country local committees are being set up to explore the possibility of co-operation in this matter. Before long I think we shall probably have the type of co-operation we need. Just how far we can go along that road remains to be seen. We have nothing to be ashamed of in the matter of our reception of refugees over the years. If my memory serves me correctly, I think that since the war years something like 180,000 refugees have been taken into this country.
More than that, I think.
My official tells me that officially the figure is 180,000. Then, of course, there were many who were not classed as refugees who came in in the regular way. Of those we have no count.
That figure of 180,000 does not include Hungarians, does it?
No.

So the figure is really about
220,000?

Yes. We had some 38,000 Hungarians. With respect to the matter of health, I might say also that of those 38,000 Hungarians who came in it is estimated by the Department of National Health and Welfare that some 900 went into hospitals. We have therefore made a considerable contribution to the solution of the refugee problem. In addition to that, I might say that cash contributions I think including this year will total over $1 million. That is another contribution that has been made by Canadians to the solution of this problem. We should like

to co-operate in this international refugee year. It comes, of course, right on the heels of the assistance which we gave to the Hungarians, a matter which was discussed in this chamber this afternoon. As I said, we shall have to wait and see what develops out of the various offers of co-operation which will be forthcoming from Canadians generally. I should like to make just one comment with regard to the oft-repeated criticism of the size of immigration last year or of the number of immigrants who came into this country last year as compared with 1958.
Does the hon. lady not mean 1957?

I mean 1957. I am sure that hon. members of this committee, when they seriously look at these figures, will realize that this is no fair comparison at all. The year 1957 was the most unusual year in the history of Canada since about 1913. As a matter of fact, the average for the last ten years, if you exclude 1957, was 153,000. Even in taking that average, you include the other bumper year of 1951 when the refugee camps in Europe were cleaned out. I therefore do not think it is reasonable to take the figure of
282.000	as a normal figure. As a matter of fact, if you take out the bumper year of 1951 and that of 1957 you have an average of some
132.000	over the last ten years, a figure which is not too far removed from the nearly 125,000 which came in last year.
In reply to the hon. member for Fort William who quoted Mr. Rhys Sale with regard to the five per cent increase, I should like to say that if he will consult the Canada Year Book he will find out that it is just about the increase that we have had in population over the past few years. It averages out to just about that figure, namely 500,000 per year, including both natural increase and immigration.
There are a couple of specific questions, Mr. Chairman-
Will the minister permit me to ask a question?
Yes.

It concerns sponsored applicants. What is the attitude of the government now with regard to young fellows who are single and who have been assured employment on their arrival here? I know of cases where their applications have been turned down.
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that I do not understand what the hon. member is talking about.

I am referring to applications from young immigrants of say 20 years of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration age or 30 years of age who are single, who wish to come out here from Italy, who have made applications; and whose applications were supported by sponsors here in Canada guaranteeing employment.

Of course the situation in Italy is probably different from that in any other country because of the terrific backlog there. I will answer the hon. member's question in the course of my remarks on this subject because it all ties in with remarks made in this chamber by various members.
It is true that during this last year immigration from the United Kingdom fell from the first place. I do not think that was so much a matter of design as of accident. It is notable that the people from the United Kingdom, once they are in this country, do not resort to the sponsoring of relatives in the same way as do immigrants from other countries. Italy is the one country which in great volume sponsors relatives. It seems that immigrants from Italy, immediately they come to this land and are here for the required length of time, want to bring out their brothers, sisters and other relatives. That has been mainly the reason for the huge backlog which has built up in Italy. I may say that it is a backlog which causes us a great deal of concern. I do think it would be a very good thing, and a good thing for another reason. It has come to my notice even since I ceased to be minister, and it came to my notice a good many times before, that every so often cases do arise, some of them very embarrassing. Without citing any names, I am going to cite one or two that have recently come to my notice. One that came to my notice the hon. lady knows about and I am not blaming her because there is nothing she can do about it any more than anyone else can, except parliament itself. But a child was brought to Canada in infancy, in fact before he was a year old, from Indiana and lived here, in fact was adopted by Canadians. He lived in Montreal all his life to the age of 23 or 24, when he found to his great embarrassment that he had never been landed as an immigrant. Therefore, he could not become a citizen for another five years. This is just an absurdity, of course, but it is the law and there is nothing whatever that the minister, the governor in council, or anybody else except parliament can do about a case like that.
It came to my attention the other day that a ship's deserter-I am sorry the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice who have such tender hearts for ships' deserters, or at any rate did have for one ship's deserter a year or two ago are not in the house at the moment-deserted his ship some 20 or 25 years ago. He has never been landed but has lived as a perfectly good resident of his community. He married a Canadian and has grown-up children in Canada. He now finds that even if he is landed, I am not sure whether he is yet, he may be faced with deportation. I have not gone into the details of the case, because again I knew that it would take five years after landing before that person could get citizenship. I must confess-perhaps I should not say this-that at the time I brought the amendment into the house when I was minister-I think in 1956-I did place a cut-off date in the bill I brought in and which was accepted by the house. It was provided that any person who had landed or been technically landed before that date but had been resident in Canada for a longer time before that could count the prior period, so that it was possible for someone who had already been here for five years to be landed and make his application for citizenship, and do the one right after the other.
I did suggest at that time that under certain safeguards and in certain circumstances we should put a provision in the act that would not be just retroactive but would

You have a suspicious nature.

I am inclined to think that that might have happened because that was in the days when the hon. lady and her friends had had no experience of government, and they did not realize that orders in council based upon legislation are perfectly proper and necessary instruments for the use of any government. We have a different kind of parliament now, with a responsible opposition that understands something about these things, and it does seem to me that we should take another look-when all is said and done-10 years have passed since the hon. member for Essex East introduced the original Canadian Citizenship Act; in fact, it is more than 10 years. It came into effect on January 1, 1947, and it does seem to me that it would be a very useful thing indeed if the hon. lady at the next session of parliament- I know she has got the Indian Act under contemplation for this session and that is enough for one session, I quite agree-would consider having a proposal laid before this house and the other place for a joint committee, and a serious committee, to go into the citizenship act in a non-partisan way in the light of our 12 or 13 years experience, with a view to trying to remove some of those anomalies and also trying to clear up this question of real equality of status. I offer this as what I hope will be a constructive suggestion.

I thereupon wrote a letter to the Prime Minister about this case, which I also propose to read into the record. The letter is dated December 31 and reads:
My dear Prime Minister:
I have been astonished to receive a reply from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to my telegram regarding the infant daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jean Volcy of Montreal flatly refusing to consider my representations. The minister in her reply completely ignores the fact that my representations were not made on behalf of Mr. and Mrs. Volcy but on behalf of their daughter who is a natural born Canadian citizen. I recognize that the parents are not admissible as immigrants under present regulations but I am also aware that hundreds of persons have been admitted as immigrants this year-
That was the year 1958.
-by order in council. You will no doubt recall your own strong appeal to me just two years ago to recommend an order in council for the admission of one George Christian Hanna who had no connection whatever with this country and who has since been deported by your government.
Here we have a case of the parents of a Canadian citizen whose deportation would involve the enforced exile or the desertion of one of our own citizens. These people have lived in Canada for some time and the public has no evidence they have committed any crime or even failed to support themselves.
The minister in her telegram says she has given exhaustive consideration to this deplorable situation which she does not define. If that means these people are not desirable immigrants, surely action should have been taken before they became the parents of a Canadian citizen.
The press reports indicate that the decision of the courts in this case was based solely on technical inadmissibility under the existing regulations which could easily be cured by an order in council.
The refusal of the minister to recommend an order in council in this case is almost certain to create the impression that the action proposed is being taken because of the colour of the skin of the parents of this Canadian citizen.
Is not this proposed action, which is surely prejudicial to the natural rights of a citizen of Canada, a strange prelude to the proposed bill of rights? I am writing to you because the minister seems to have overlooked altogether the fact that her action will affect the rights and the welfare of a citizen of Canada. I am of course sending the minister a copy of my letter.
In due course I received an acknowledgement from the Prime Minister's office saying that the case was before the courts. I am relying here on my recollection and it is possible that my recollection will turn out to be wrong. I admit at once that many times during the period when I was minister deportation orders were issued against the parents of a Canadian citizen but because there was no appeal or anything of that sort they

never came to my attention. I am not going to say for a minute that there may not have been some parents of Canadian citizens deported while I was minister and that they may not have taken their children with them, but during that period I cannot recall any case ever brought to my attention where the deportation of the parents would involve either separation from an infant child or the taking of that child out of Canada into exile that I did not stay the operation of the deportation order at once.

No attempt should be made to carry it out, and unless there are the strongest possible reasons against it action should be taken by the governor in council under the act to land the parents of that Canadian citizen as immigrants.
Although it seems to me that the rights of a Canadian citizen are of the utmost importance, this is by no means merely a question of rights but a question of the practical application as well. The hon. lady, who is a lot younger than I am, perhaps will not remember that 25 years ago or 27 years ago or up to 30 years ago, when her political friends were in office in this country, a great number of residents of Canada were deported, particularly to the United Kingdom, from some parts of the prairie provinces because they had become public charges. I happen to recall some of these cases personally. I particularly remember a number from the city of Saskatoon. The action created a great deal of stir at that time. Years later, after the wider extension of assisted passages for immigrants from the United Kingdom, we found that we were receiving applications from people who could not qualify for assistance as immigrants because they were Canadian citizens who had been born in Canada, who had gone to the United Kingdom because their parents had been deported but who, as natural born Canadian citizens, could not be classed as immigrants and therefore could not get assistance to come to their own country. That situation was remedied by parliament without any difficulty whatsoever.
What is going to happen in practical effect if we deport-I should not say "deport" because we cannot deport them-if we exile these Canadian citizens is that they are going to grow up in another country while having all the rights of a Canadian citizen, and in
many cases they are going to want to exercise those rights years later. In looking at the citizenship act, section 22, if I could refer to it to preface my other remarks, we find a Canadian citizen, whether natural born or naturalized is entitled to rights, powers and privileges and is subject to all obligations, duties and liabilities. I underline those words, rights, powers and privileges as well as obligations, duties and liabilities.
I do not know if anyone has made a complete and all-embracing statement as to what is entailed in those rights and obligations. I doubt if such a complete compilation has been made. I am sure that those things sort of constitute our whole fabric of society and change from time to time through the process of time itself as well as a result of legislation and court decisions.
These rights and these obligations that devolve upon Canadian citizens are-or should be, anyway-equally applicable to British Columbia, the province from which I come and right across Canada to Newfoundland. No matter which province a person happens to be resident in, the rights and the obligations he has should be equitable throughout all of the provinces. I think we can assume that one of the fundamental and inalienable rights which we have-and which I mentioned earlier today at another stage of the proceedings-is contained in one of the conventions of the international labour organization at its 31st session in 1948, 11 years ago. While it is true that Canada has not ratified it-something which I think is a failure on the part of the government of Canada, both the one we had previously and this one-this convention concerns the freedom of association and the protection of the right to organize which I submit falls within
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration one of the fundamental rights, powers, privileges, obligations and duties set out in section 22 of the act. The article of that convention has specific reference to the happenings of the last day or two in one of the provinces of Canada. I refer to article 4 which I am going to quote again. It states:
Workers' and employers' organizations shall not be liable to be dissolved or suspended by administrative authority.
Article 11 I should say has specific reference. It states:
Each member of the international labour organization for which this convention is in force-
I admit, as I said earlier, that it is not in force because of failure of this government and the previous Liberal government to ratify it.
-undertakes to take all necessary and appropriate measures to ensure that workers and employers may exercise freely the right to organize.
That is one of the rights of citizens in Canada as set out in this international labour convention, section 4.

56. Administration, $680,907.

If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks. I think possibly I should give some information to the committee. The 1959-60 main estimates for Indian affairs show an increase of $6,563,652 over 1958-59. The major portion of

this increase is attributable to two basically important fields, namely education and welfare of Indians.
The total increase in operating costs for education is $2,928,886 and for welfare $2,322,104. This envisages the employment of 42 additional teachers at day schools and 32 at residential or a total increase in teaching staff of 74. There is an increase of $350,000 to further assist in the education of Indian children in association with non-Indians and: an additional amount of $765,499 to finance the operation and maintenance of residential schools. The program of residential school construction calls for an additional amount of $795,300 over 1958-59. The increase in the welfare appropriation is largely due to increased requirements to meet relief costs and the care of indigents.
In the all important field of education good progress has been made. For example, in the 1958-59 fiscal year the unrevised figures show a total enrolment of 38,836 Indian pupils in all schools. This includes 8,429 pupils who attend non-Indian schools, universities, teachers' colleges and commercial or trade schools and represents an increase of 1,099 over the previous year. The estimates presented for consideration visualize a further increase in numbers and further participation by Indian pupils in higher education.
In the past academic year we have had about 2,500 students taking post-elementary school training. There were but 200 in 1948 and it is my hope that this tenfold increase will gather momentum with each year. To this end a system of scholarships offers further incentive to Indian students to continue their education. These scholarships, representing a total value of $25,000, are offered in addition to the normal assistance given at post-elementary school level. Thirteen awards were made in the current year.
In both Indian day and residential schools the practical arts courses such as home economics, woodwork, sheet metal work, et cetera enrolled 5,898 students. For this program 48 instructors were employed for classes enrolling 2,683 boys. For the girls 63 teachers were employed to give instruction in home economics to over 3,215 students.
It is planned to construct 88 classrooms together with other necessary construction including teachers' residences. In line with the efforts being made to educate Indian children in association with non-Indians, provision is made for contributions towards the construction of 11 joint schools.
The residential school construction program, designed to take care of children of northern migratory Indians and those from broken homes, shows an increase. It includes

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
two hostels for children attending elementary and high schools in Whitehorse and a start on the replacement of one old school, namely St. Mary's residential school, New Westminster agency, British Columbia.
In the field of Indian housing the appropriation was doubled in 1958-59 when the amount of $2 million was provided. This has made possible an expanded program of housing construction and an improved standard of housing, as well as an increased number of cost sharing agreements with bands with sufficient funds to participate in such undertakings. During 1958-59 a survey of housing was undertaken which will have an important bearing on the building program in future. The emphasis on financial assistance to Indians in northern and remote areas will continue.
In 1959-60 it is proposed to maintain the expenditure at the same level of $2 million and it is estimated this will cover the financing in whole or in part of close to 1,000 housing units. On the average for every dollar expended from public funds in recent years there has been an equal or greater amount provided from personal contributions by the Indians themselves in the form of labour, cash and materials, band funds, and Veterans Land Act grants available to Indian veterans.
During the debate on the departmental estimates in the last session of this house the question of the quantity of relief supplied on behalf of Indians in need was raised by some hon. members opposite. I said at that time that this subject was under constant review. As a result of a thorough and careful study improved standards and revised procedures of relief administration on behalf of Indians are being introduced throughout the country on April 1 next, in order that Indians in destitute circumstances may receive, as nearly as possible, the same treatment and assistance available for non-Indians in need in Canadian communities generally.
As I informed hon. members last year, the department in 1957 embarked upon a limited experimental program in the payment of relief in cash and in dollar value orders, replacing relief in kind according to a ration scale. This experiment has proven to be successful and on the basis of this experience and following a comprehensive review of scales of assistance and procedures in effect in various provinces and non-Indian communities throughout Canada, these methods are tot be adopted universally with effect April 1 next.
At the same time new scales of food allowances in terms of dollar value have been authorized, which represent a substantial advance over the retail value of the foods
listed on the former ration scale, and an increase over the rates payable in the experimental projects which have been in force since 1957.
These changes are costly, as evidenced by the fact that provision is made for expenditures of approximately $3 million in excess of those incurred in 1957-58. It is considered essential, however, that adequate assistance be provided for Indians in need in order that they may maintain a satisfactory standard of living at times when they are unable to do this through their own efforts. It is also the purpose of these changes to bring procedures and standards of assistance in line with those in force in non-Indian communities; to give greater responsibility to the Indians in the management of their own affairs.

An important change in branch organization has resulted from the recent establishment of an economic development division which is now in the process of being staffed. The establishment of this separate division is reflected in the introduction of two new votes which encompass a number of items concerned with fur development, agriculture, urban-type employment and other commercial enterprises designed to permit the attainment by Indians of a higher standard of living. A placement program is now in operation with the object of assisting Indians to find employment in a wider range of fields than has hitherto been open to them. Placement officers are now employed in six of the eight administrative regions, with a senior placement officer in Ottawa, and it is planned in 1959-60 to engage two more such officers, one

Group placements in seasonal employment have been increasingly successful. In addition, in the last two fiscal years special arrangements were made for the employment of Indians in clearing of roads in the Yellow-knife-Fort Rae area of the Northwest Territories.

Mr. Chairman, in the few moments at my disposal, having listened to the minister as carefully as I could, I would like to express at least my own sincere appreciation for her having made the changes in the matters of welfare cash payments, the increases toward education and educational facilities, and so on, which she has just announced. In the last couple of sessions I have had occasion to complain about some of these matters, particularly the inadequate food rationing arrangements which applied to Indians. I am very pleased about this, and I am sure that many of our native Indian people who have occasion to call on this service of the department will be appreciative too. The minister is taking a much more progressive attitude toward this phase of our Indian problems than has been taken for quite a number of years. Some of these grievances have been of very, very long standing with the Indian people, and I am sure this is only the first step toward giving Indians the opportunity to play the fullest possible role in society.
I hope you will excuse me, Mr. Chairman, if I make brief mention of a notice of motion that is now on the order paper with respect to the establishment of a joint committee of this house and the other place to deal with Indian affairs. I notice that it is almost a month or four and a half weeks ago that notice of this motion was given, and I hope it will not be too long delayed before we are able to proceed with the motion in the name of the hon. minister and that this joint committee is established to deal with the Indian Act and Indian affairs in general.
There is one phase, education, which probably in importance overshadows the long range views with respect to our hopes and desires for all Indian people, and probably even overshadows all of the other activities of the Indian affairs branch of the department, and of course takes into account the educational facilities of the various provinces and of private organizations. I would like,

if I may, on this question of education, to-point out again, if it is necessary to point it out, that the desire for education on the part of Indians has been of long standing.
In 1916 a royal commission on Indian affairs was established in the province of British Columbia, and I have a copy of one of the volumes of its report. This 1916 royal commission was not appointed, incidentally, to deal with the question of education, but was appointed to deal with the question of delineating certain areas for reserves for particular bands and also the question of rights of way through Indian reserves or property for a railroad. I point out that the specific object of this royal commission in British Columbia in 1916, which is long before many of the members sitting in this house today were even born-certainly some years before I was born-was not to deal with education but to deal with the delineation of reserves. However, in the process of that they compiled a certain amount of information about population of bands, the occupation of people in those bands, the condition of them, the educational facilities, the head of the families, how many people under 19, and so on, giving quite a statistical analysis of the population of each band.
I would like to point to some of the comments which are made in this report of 1916, some 43 years ago, and the incidental references the commission made to education of Indian bands and the desire of Indians to obtain that education. In the riding which I represent there is quite a large population of native Indian people, and I wish to refer to how, 43 years ago, native Indians had this attitude toward education. Now we are very slowly and finally realizing the ideals and hopes they had at that time. In the report reference is made to the Kitseguecla band and their condition. It says that they are progressive and comfortably situated. With respect to the view of the Indians on education it says that Indians are understood to strongly favour industrial schools. As I say, this was some 43 years ago, and the Indian people in that reservation at Kitseguecla were desirous of some form of educational facilities in the way of industrial schools. Then there is reference to the Kitamaat band and their condition. This was long before many of us in this house were born, and long before our parents thought we would be entering schools and proceeding through the various steps of education.

subtopic: NOTE FROM CANADIAN CHARGE D'AFFAIRES, WASHINGTON, TO ACTING SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext: Canadian Embassy

The Canadian charge d'affaires ad interim presents his compliments to the acting secretary of state and has the honour to refer to the matter of restrictions affecting exports of oil from Canada to the United States and in particular to the recent proposal on which the administrator of the voluntary oil import program has requested comment.
The notes of the Canadian ambassador to the Secretary of State dated January 15 and June 23, 1958, set forth the views of the Canadian government on the principles involved in such restrictive measures. It would now appear desirable to restate these views in the light of the proposal for revision of the basis of the import restrictions which has been put forward for discussion by the administrator of the voluntary oil import program.
The Canadian government continues to believe that there can be no justification on grounds of security (or, for that matter, on other grounds) for United States restrictions on oil coming from Canada. United States government restrictions on oil imports from Canada, imposed in peacetime for security reasons, are not reconcilable with the need of Canada and the United States to pool their oil resources in time of common emergency.
The Canadian government acknowledges that the proposal by the administrator of the voluntary oil import program attempts to take into account the importance to Canada of exports of oil to the United States, and the importance to United States refineries operating on Canadian crude oil of continued freedom to use that oil. Section 5(d) of the proposal would appear to offer to refineries in district II using Canadian oil some means of mitigating the very damaging effects of other sections of the new proposal.
The Canadian government would point out, however, that application of section 5(d) would be a matter of administrative discretion, rather than formal directive. The Canadian government is also aware that the United States government is subject to very considerable pressures from interests which would seek to make the oil import program more rather than less restrictive. The United States government will therefore understand that while the Canadian 66968-9-106$
government is appreciative of the consideration shown for the Canadian position, the Canadian government could only await the actual outcome of the proposed revision with concern.
Further, the Canadian government would not wish any comments on the current proposal to be taken to imply a preference on the part of the Canadian government for one basis of import restrictions as against another. Furthermore so long as any import restrictions continue to be applied against Canadian oil, they will have a deleterious effect on Canadian-United States relations.
Following the imposition of United States restrictions imports from Canada have not only fallen sharply but have declined more seriously than imports from other areas supplying oil to the United States. Examination of United States import figures for petroleum and its products for the months from July 1957 indicates that the volume of crude oil and products moving from Venezuela and the Netherlands Antilles together to the United States has continued fairly level; a decline in crude oil imports has been offset by increases in imports of products. Middle Eastern crude oil and product sales have declined somewhat. In contrast, Canadian sales of crude and products have declined sharply, and by May 1958 were less than half the volume of July 1957. In July, 1957 Canada supplied 9.5 per cent of total United States imports of crude oil and products; by May, 1958 Canada was supplying only 4.5 per cent of such imports. Thus, imports from Canada, the most secure outside source of oil for the United States in normal times and in times of emergency, have fallen much more than those from offshore areas since the inauguration of the United States program established on grounds of United States national security.
This disproportionate decline would appear to have come about largely because of indirect effects of the United States program.
In district V, offshore oil from various sources, after it was denied ready access to the United States eastern seaboard and California, has virtually displaced Canadian oil in Puget sound. It would appear that the Puget sound refiners, having been limited as to the amount of crude oil they could import, have tended to disregard other considerations and have turned to the cheapest available sources of imported oil-Venezuela, the Middle East

and the Far East-partly to offset the uneconomic use of United States domestic crude brought in from California; in an open market they might well have continued to use a substantial proportion of Canadian oil.
Similarly, in district II, Venezuelan oil, when limited in its access to other markets in the United States, has been displacing Canadian oil, though the displacement has been less than in the case of district V.
The United States import program has thus borne most heavily upon the source of imported oil for the United States which would be least subject to interruption, and which is most akin to the United States in the cost structure and market prorationing arrangements of its oil industry. Canadian oil is not and has not been a factor contributing to the problems which led to the institution of the United States oil import program. It is therefore a matter of regret and concern to the Canadian government that, notwithstanding the unquestioned goodwill of the United States government, the Canadian oil industry should not only suffer from the import restrictions but
should suffer more than the oil industries of other areas especially since the Canadian industry cannot be regarded as having contributed to the problems intended to be met by the United States oil import program. The United States government will recall that in its note of February 19, 1958, it expressed the view that strong petroleum industries in both countries "contribute importantly to the support of the defence efforts with which both Canada and the United States are associated".
In the light of the considerations set out above, it is the hope of the Canadian government that, both because of the current adverse effects and because of the potential consequences for future petroleum policies, the government of the United States in its current re-examination of the import program will find itself able to remove the restrictions which have been imposed on the access of Canadian oil to markets in the United States.
A. E. Ritchie
The Canadian Embassy,
Washington, D. C.
October 20, 1958.
